Take the Malton plant. A change was made recently in this plant. There has been something seriously wrong with the production of aircraft in this plant right from the beginning of the war. And the minister acted. In November last he had the plant expropriated and the government obtained outright ownership from that date. The men who operated this plant were paid $4,000,000 therefor, and the government assumed the liabilities in connection with the plant as of that date, liabilities which are estimated at $1,760,000. The sessional paper states:
All amounts allowed or allowable to the company by way of depreciation .	.	. will be
absorbed in the costs of production of planes manufactured and delivered up to that date.
Special depreciation was taken into consideration in the amount of $2,253,597, and normal depreciation of $791,856.
To-day I think we are entitled to information as to how many planes ever came out of this plant. What is the record? What was the cost per plane? What are the comparative unit costs in this particular plant as compared with plants in the United States?
Let me point out furthermore that this company, the National Steel Car company, made profits during the period it was in operation. The net profits from June 30, 1942, to November 5, 1942, were estimated at $513,665. The return continues:
. . . that was partly the company's estimate of the profit it hoped would be allowed on contracts providing for audited cost plus a profit mutually acceptable to the government and the company as a fair and reasonable profit.
The question I should like to ask in that connection is, what was the percentage of profit that was finally agreed upon as mutually acceptable to the government and the company?
War Appropriation-Supplies
That is set out in the order in council. It has been tabled.
Yes; those details are set out, but not the particulars I have asked for.
Oh, yes.

If my understanding is correct, the only particulars that are set out in the order in council are those giving the information I have already mentioned. The total cost of the work received by this plant from the inception to November 5, 1942, was $18,935,472, or almost $19,000,000. It will be a very simple matter, if the minister informs the committee how many planes have been turned out of the different types, to compute whether this plant was efficiently operated.

And deduct the stocks on
hand.

That is perfectly
true: there would be a deduction of the stocks on hand. The general impression among those who are in a position to know is that this plant did not operate efficiently and was permitted to continue so to operate for a ' long period of time after it must have been realized by the government or the controller that such was the situation.
I realize that the government made no capital advances to this company, but it did provide assistance for machinery, jigs and tools, and the like. What was the value thereof? What control did the government have over the supplies that it gave this plant? Has the amount of the indebtedness of this plant been finally determined yet? Furthermore, even after the taking over of the plant, has there been a continuing small production or the assembling of the bombers that are to be produced there? What is the situation?
We were given to understand, if the press reports were correct, that a Lancaster bomber was expected to be produced in the month of April. The date is now, I believe, a good deal later than that, certainly not during the present month. All these things point to laxity or delay which requires reorganization if Canada is to contribute her share in the aircraft division of the minister's department.
Is there any reason Why there should not be set up to-day an advisory committee of industrialists trained in aircraft production, or in other production, to assist the present controller? For the record during the past two years, during the period of the control of Mr. R. B. Bell has been such that in my

opinion any fair-minded man must agree that some change, some addition, some counsel must be given him.
I pass on to the matter of the de Havilland plant. All we know about that is that recently a controller was placed in charge of this plant. He has wide authority and is assisted by an advisory board. What are the facts in this connection? Why were changes made? What has been the record of the de Havilland corporation in the production of aeroplanes? These are matters that cannot be helpful to the enemy. The information I ask for is given daily in the United States of America. Production is stated month by month.
For each plant?
The total production is stated. We visited recently two plants in Buffalo producing types of fighter planes and there was no attempt at concealment of production.
Oh, yes.
Did you get that information in Buffalo?
Yes. I was present with five others at the time the statement was made.
Tell us what it is.

I am not going
to be brought into that. I will tell the minister.
It is an approximation.
I can tell the minister.

I can tell the hon. member
what it is, but I get it in the strictest confidence myself. It is a secret list. It is carefully guarded in every country.
As an hon. member says, it is approximate.

Some of the rest of us
could not get it.

Do not blame him for
that.

I should like information with regard to production since 1942. Is this house and is the country not entitled to information as to production of these planes? According to the press the minister from Canada to Australia gave production figures. Why should we not have information in this house?

He is a good man to give it because he does not know what it is. He cannot violate secrecy there.

War Appropriation-Supplies

If the minister of Canada to Australia did not know what he was talking about, that is a tribute coming from the Minister of Munitions and Supply to the appointment of the representative of this government in our sister dominion. In any^ event, let us have the record prior to September, 1942, in this plant. How many man-hours were taken in the production of planes in this plant? I know the minister has devoted himself to his duties. No one will pay a higher tribute to him for devotion to his job, and in what I am saying I am interested in the improvement of the situation. Many of the criticisms from this side of the house have been so accepted by the government in the past. The only way in which this situation with regard to aircraft will be improved is by adopting the attitude taken by this apposition, asking for information and demanding improvement. In Britain it was Beaverbrook; it was members on the government side of the house, who in May, June and July, 1940, in season and out of season, put before the government the necessity of expanding the war programme. They were told by members of the government that all was well, but they knew differently. It is in that spirit of service that I bring the situation to the attention of this committee.
If these factories are not producing what they should, we should know the reason why. The management in the Malton plant were not removed just for the amusement of the department. The-change in the de Havilland plant and the substitution of Mr. Glassco as controller was not made unless there was a reason. Changes were justified, and in the set-up within the Department of Munitions and Supply there should be an aircraft advisory committee similar to those which have done such magnificent work in certain other fields of production. I am not going to say more at this time, except to point out that the appointment of Mr. Glassco as controller indicates that inefficiency did characterize the operation of this plant.
Unless these matters are brought before parliament, as members of the opposition have the right and responsibility to bring them before parliament, how are we to know that the same conditions will not prevail and continue next year? I am asking the minister, within the confines of public security, to give these figures: how many man-hours were required for the production of each type of plane manufactured by these two companies during the past year? If he cannot give us the record as to the number of planes, and apparently he has taken the stand that
he will not do so, in spite of the fact that he stated that this plant is expected to produce five Mosquito bombers very shortly-
I will give the hon. member quite a lot of information.
Then we have been arguing at cross-purposes.
I have not been arguing. I have been saying that the situation in the United States was not just as easy as the hon. member was suggesting.
The minister indicated that this information might not be given.
I did not say so.

Then we can get the information. When we read between the lines of the order in council appointing Mr. Glassco, as I say it must be obvious that this plant failed to do its duty; and the circumstances in connection with the taking over of the National Steel Car plant are equally indicative of the same condition. The order in council appointing Mr. Glassco under date of June 7, gives him exclusive power, in conjunction with certain assistants, to operate this plant. In that work he will be a servant of the Department of Munitions and Supply and be under the control of Mr. Bell. Parliament has a right to full information in this regard.
As I remember the minister's statement the other day, it was that there had been a continuing increase in the production of aircraft in Canada since the beginning of the war. I pointed out that a year ago we had the same nine types of' planes we are producing to-day; yet now we are producing approximately eighty planes less per month than we were producing at that time. The reply was that in point of tonnage there would be an increase. If that is so, let us have the record for 1941 as to the tonnage of planes produced in Canada and the record for 1942 in that connection. I do say that since other of the organizations and agencies under the Department of Munitions and Supply have arrived at the point of full production, having regard to the need for aircraft both now and in the period after the war, attention should be concentrated now to the end that the conditions which have been prevalent in this country in connection wth aircraft production shall no longer continue to exist.

I have been waiting for some time for an opportunity to answer some of the questions that have been asked. There

War Appropriation-Supplies
seemed to be two inquiries, one as to the National Steel Car plant, which is now called Victory Aircraft, and the other in regard to the de Havilland plant. First let me mention the controller of aircraft. As the hon. gentleman has said, we have fifteen controllers, but Mr. Bell acts in a dual capacity. As controller of aircraft his duties are very light; he simply has the power to determine what the facilities of the aircraft industry will be used for. It is as director-general of aircraft production that he directs the production of aeroplanes. While he has no committee as controller, he has a committee as director-general.
Who are on his committee as director-general?
It is a committee representing all the aircraft branches; I could not tell the names.
Could we get that list?

Yes, I shall be glad to get it, and we have the production committee under the Department of Munitions and Supply, of which Mr. Bell is a member, under the chairmanship of Mr. Carmichael, and. that committee also gives a good deal of attention to the aircraft situation, I do not think the hon. member intentionally lech the committee astray when he said that a year ago I mentioned that we were down to nine types of planes. We announced a programme for the future, of nine types of planes.
No.
Read your Hansard. At that time we had many more than nine types of planes.

On a point of order, on May 14, 1942, at page 2435 of Hansard the minister said:	*
We have now reduced our production to nine types of planes, and the plants are cleaning up old orders and concentrating on one type of production for each plant with accordingly improved results.
Those are the minister's words.

That is what I say. We were cleaning up old orders, for other than the nine types of planes; we were making a number of planes of which we have gone out of production in the last two or three months. In other words, we have cleaned up the programme. Our objective has been to get down to a production of nine types of planes. Unfortunately, two or three of these planes are not in production yet. From the time you get

the blueprints of a plane and undertake its manufacture, a certain period must elapse which, for some reason or another, which I cannot explain, is fifteen months. We can set our objective at eleven months, twelve months, or anything else, but from the time we undertake the production of a new plane until that plane is rolling out at maximum volume, the elapsed time is about fifteen months. That interval seems to be inevitable.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Before recess I was discussing the time taken to bring new planes into production.
The gestation period.

Yes, although I see no reference to that in Hansard. As a matter of fact, the new programme is not fully in production as yet. We are producing the new trainer planes included in the programme to full capacity, except in respect of the Anson. I refer to a new type of Anson, and it is not up to full capacity, owing to drastic changes in the type of fuselage. It is now being made of plastics instead of metal, and the plastics plant is not operating to full capacity. However, the trainer programme is well under way, and it is just a matter of weeks until that programme is running at full capacity.
In respect of combat planes I would say the PBY Catalina flying boat programme is progressing favourably. It is not fully up to capacity, but the fact remains that we have turned out a large number of Catalinas. We are not particularly worried about that programme.
The Mosquito programme has been sticky. I think we underestimated the time necessary to get into full production on that item. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) asked how many Mosquitoes we had turned out. At the end of last week twenty-one had been accepted. The production is not stepping up as rapidly as we had hoped; but the components plants are now operating well up to capacity, and I think it is only a matter of weeks until we shall have production approaching the objective.
In respect of the Lancaster bomber we are getting very close to production. In about

War Appropriation-Supplies
two or three weeks the first completed Lancaster bomber will be test-flown, and it will be only a matter of hours until the second plane will come off the end of the assembly line.
The navy dive bomber is not in production as yet. There have been many changes in design, and I would hesitate to say just when the navy bomber programme will be well under way-. Two plants are engaged in this programme.
Is that a plane of United States design?

Yes, it is designed by the Curtiss company.	_	_
I now direct my attention to the transaction which resulted in the government acquiring the plant -of the National Steel Car company. The aeroplane plant of National Steel Cat was a privately built and privately owned plant. It had had a rather unsatisfactory career, so far as management was concerned. There had been a number of changes in management. Finally the department took a hand in the situation and persuaded another firm to give up a very experienced manager. National Steel Car undertook to place this manager in control of the plant, under certain terms agreed upon between themselves and the Department of Munitions and Supply.
The crisis occurred when, without warning to the Department of Munitions and Supply, this new general manager was dismissed by the directors. I might point out that in the meantime Mr. Magor, chairman of the board of the company had died. The fact that arrangements covering the new management were made directly with Mr. Magor, and involved his personal attention had, I think, some bearing on the situation which developed. I think if Mr. Magor had been in charge the situation would not have arisen. However, it did arise, and1 the board of directors dismissed the manager, and made no suggestion as to any replacement.

How long had the
manager been there before he was dismissed?

I cannot say, but I would estimate that it would be perhaps ten or eleven months. We received petitions from the men in the plant demanding that the manager be retained, and saying that a general strike would occur if he were not retained. We received a letter signed by a great number of the office workers asking that the general manager be retained. After some discussion with the directors the government decided to expropriate the plant. As a result the plant was expropriated, and a
crown company was formed, with Mr. Bickell as president, and with the general manager who had been dismissed as general manager.
I believe I can report to the committee that subsequent events have justified the action taken by the government. Many people well-qualified to judge have visited the plant recently, and have told me that the organization is shaping up splendidly, and that it will be able to produce in volume when the flow of planes begins. I am told that to-day it is a first-class plant.
On the financial side I might explain that we took over the property as a going concern. We went back to the building of the plant, and used the actual building costs. We subtracted from the building costs the depreciation that had been paid to the owners by way of accelerated depreciation. We took account of the profits-possibly I should not say we took account of the profits; we simply took the revenues and expenditures, and we treated the profits as a separate item, and fixed our own margin of profit for the full period that the plant had been operated. We took the stocks in hand and checked them against the books. We took over the assets and liabilities of the company, as a going concern, at an agreed upon price, the details of which are covered fully in the order in council which has been tabled in the house.
What was the rate of profit?
I have not the order in council before me. Has my hon. friend a copy of it?
I have not it here.
It is two or three hundred thousand dollars.
What was the rate?
There was no rate. We simply assessed the work that had been done, and placed on it a profit we considered reasonable. Probably I shall be in a position to give more exact information later on.
The company had never been in actual production?
Yes, it had produced.
I am glad to be corrected on that.

Yes; it is difficult to represent production as a definite number of planes. A certain number of planes were built. They built Lysanders. An order of Lysanders, for both Canadian and- British governments, was built at the plant. It -was also engaged on the Anson production. Then, it was engaged
War Appropriation-Supplies

on Hampden and Hurricane wings. As my hon. friend knows-perhaps I should tell him -this plant was in a group of six plants which produced the Hampden bomber. Its part of the Hampden work was completed, as well as the order for Lysanders, and some 200 Anson planes. They were actually built and turned out at the plant. In addition, the plant did a large volume of work on spare parts for Canadian and British orders, and also assembly and overhaul work on Canadian planes.
What was the specific charge against the previous management? I do not think that was ever made clear.

There was no charge against the previous management, but a board of directors cannot operate a plant efficiently except through a general manager. The board of directors dismissed the general manager whom we had gone to great effort to provide for them and who haid an excellent record in Canada as a producer of aeroplanes. They had no replacement in hand, and they had no suggestion of replacement.
What was the explanation for the dismissal?
That he would not carry out the orders of the board of directors. I believe it was an internal quarrel.
To keep production up to a certain point?
No; it had nothing whatever to do with production.
What was the charge against the previous general manager who did not satisfy the government?

He was not dismissed by the government; he was dismissed by the board of directors.
_ Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): Then you intervened. He was let out because you were not satisfied.
Oh, no. Does my hon. friend mean the last general manager?
I mean the man previous to the man you brought in.

They were without a general manager when we took David Boyd from Canadian Car and Foundry and made an arrangement with Mr. Magor that he would be general manager of the plant. To-day the plant is an efficiently operated unit. The

first Lancaster bomber will come off the assembly line within a matter of two or three weeks. The plant is completely jigged up and there will be substantial production.
The minister has said that the expropriated price was an agreed price. How did that affect the shareholders? Did they suffer a capital loss, or were they protected?
They got their money back.

And a
profit?
And a profit.
They were well looked after.
They always are.
They got their money back by way of accelerated depreciation paid while they owned the plant, plus the balance which was paid when the plant was taken over.
They lost nothing.

So much for Victory Aircraft. The de Havilland plant is a subsidiary of the de Havilland Company of the United Kingdom. This plant had an excellent record. It was perhaps the largest of the pre-war aircraft plants. It was building the Moth plane before the war and it was first in the production of the Moth trainer, of which a great number were needed by the air force. Both the Moth and the Fleet were manufactured before the war and therefore the primary trainer was never a problem as far as supply was concerned. The de Havilland Company undertook a large share of the Anson programme and that was carried out in first-class style. Perhaps the performance of de Havilland on the Anson contract was the best of any of the several plants that were building that plane.
The plant then undertook to organize a very large operation in the building of the Mosquito bomber. This involved subcontracting on a large scale and the organizing of the de Havilland plant for final assembly. Certain objectives were set, but those objectives were not attained. The department put pressure upon the directors and the management of the plant to put their house in order and to obtain production. Differences arose between the management of the plant and the Canadian members of the board of directors-the board was made up of seven members, of whom three were British and four were Canadian, very responsible business men-and these differences reached the point

War Appropriation-Supplies
where the four Canadian directors sent in their resignations. AVe attempted to get the British company to intervene and straighten out the situation, but no action was taken, and finally the Canadian government stepped in and appointed a controller for the plant, with the Canadian directors a committee to act as advisers to the controller.
The controller believes that with the authority of his position he can straighten out the management troubles. There now has been some change in management and we believe that the controllership will be helpful. As soon as we are satisfied that the management has been properly reorganized, the intention is that the controllership will be lifted. After it has been reorganized, the board of directors of de Havilland will be in charge of the plant.

Has a new general
manager been appointed, or has the old one been removed?
I am not in full possession of the facts of the situation since the controller was appointed.
The de Havilland is to be operated as a private company?

It is a private company being operated under a controller appointed by the government. My hon. friend asked for the number of man-hours and the number of planes, his idea being that we, could divide the dollars put into the plant by the number of planes produced and know exactly the cost of a plane. Unfortunately it is not that simple. On its Mosquito work I do not suppose the de Havilland plant produces more than twenty-five per cent of the total value of the plane. For example the complete fuselage for the Mosquito is being produced in the plant of General Motors at Oshawa, and the wings are being produced in one of the plants of Massey-Harris. Various other parts of the Mosquito are being produced in other shops in Canada. If we took the number of dollars that have been paid to de Havilland for the work carried on in this plant and divided them by the number of planes produced, we would get a very ,low-cost plane. No study is possible as yet of the man-hours used in producing the Mosquito, because to date the work has largely been the production of components. A man-hour study is possible only when the assembly line is rolling at somewhere near capacity.
What will be the capacity of the assembly line?

We hope to get a production of five planes a day or 150 planes a month. My hon. friend will see that it will take some
speeding up to reach that figure, but that is the capacity for which we have organized, not only at de Havilland but at the component shops. As to the cost of planes produced in Canada, we have taken contracts from the United States for planes which are common types, such as the Harvard which is used by our air training plan as well as 'by the air training plan in the United States. We took the Harvard contract at the standard United States price and have had no difficulty in producing at that price. We took a Catalina flying boat contract at a competitive price and we are manufacturing for the Canadian as well as for the United States government. We are building the Anson plane in Canada. It is of Canadian design and is being bought by the United: States government. Evidently they believe that our production price is reasonable for that plane; at least we had no difficulty in signing a contract with the United States government at our production prices. As for the efficiency of our plants, where they are operating at anything like capacity, they compare favourably with anything built on this continent.

Do the plans contemplate the building of any
helicopters?
No.
You are just going to buy them from the United States?
The helicopter is a machine of the future. No helicopter has been built that is in actual combat service.
The British are using them for convoy work.
They are using them or talking of using them? So far as I know, no helicopter has been used in combat service, but there are one or two under test.

A statement was made public in Vancouver at the time there was trouble at the Boeing aircraft plant on Sea island, and according to a newspaper circulated in the district of Richmond certain charges were made by Elgin Ruddell, shop steward of Aeronautical Lodge No. 756 in the presence, it is stated, of an estimated 20,000 people. The statement alleged to have been made is this:	.
Production of P.B.Y. bombers at Boeing Aircraft of Canada Ltd. is ten months behind schedule, and the 54 bombers already built have been rejected.
I know that after that statement was made, some of the test pilots who test the planes when they are ready for acceptance by the
War Appropriation-Supplies

government contradicted that statement of the shop steward, but I want to tell the minister and the committee that a statement of that kind had an extremely damaging effect, and I think the minister should now make a public statement to the committee so that the matter can be put straight on the record. Following this charge, I made an investigation and I was given to understand by the management of the plant that the charge made was entirely untrue. After all, however, facts are facts, and I wonder whether the minister would be good enough to make a statement in the house regarding the charge that production of PBY. bombers at that plant was ten months behind schedule and that fifty-four bombers already built have been rejected.

The charge was absolutely unfounded. The Gatalinas go into active service as soon as they are accepted at the plant. When the statement was made the management naturally were disturbed. Affidavits were obtained from the test pilots who had tested the planes and also from the Royal Canadian Air Force inspectors who are responsible for checking the planes out of die plant into service. The affidavits were ,o the effect that there was not a word of wuth in the statement. There could not be. We would know about it, if there were any truth in the charge.
The minister has stated that Canada is able to compete with prices in the United States in the production of aircraft. Am I correct in that?
We are not only able to do it; we are doing it.

Why, then, should Canada not now expand her aircraft production far and beyond what it is to-day? I pointed out this afternoon the fact that in the United States of America one-quarter of the production expenditure this year on the whole United States war programme is for the production of aeroplanes. In other words, this year, according to the estimates given, 100,000 aeroplanes are to be produced in the United States, many of which will be cargocarrying planes. Canada as yet has not gone in for cargo-carrying planes, nor has it made any preparations for the after-the-war period when cargo-carrying planes must necessarily be produced on a very largely extended basis. We are just entering the era when Canada to all intents and purposes is becoming the geopolitical centre of the world in air transport. To date our production of aircraft has been small, relatively speaking to production 
in other phases of our war effort. Only the other day I was reading the figures connected with cargo-carrying planes in Canada, which indicated how important this traffic was before the war and how very much more important it will be after the war. These figures show that in 1920 the total amount of freight, et cetera, that was carried in Canadian aircraft was a matter of only 6,740 pounds. That figure rose until in 1936, 22,947,000 pounds of freight and cargo were carried. Even in 1941, with the tremendous reduction in cargocarrying into the north country compared with what we had in peace times, over 16,545,000 pounds of freight was carried. This is a matter that is receiving the attention of all the united nations but as yet there has been no declaration on the part of Canada. The United States is producing almost exclusively all the cargo-^carrying planes produced in North America. I would ask the minister to explain why it is that Canada is concentrating on the production of bombers of the types he named and why no part of our production programme includes cargo-carrying planes. Are arrangements now being made by the joint production board of the United States and Canada whereby, when hostilities are over and the prospect of post-war trade arises, Canada will have her share of the aircraft necessary for her participation in the tremendous expansion that will take place after the war?
I should like also to have an explanation from the minister in regard to the question which I raised the other day, and) which I repeat. If we have arrived at a position in Canada where we can compete with production in the United States of America, why should we not now launch out into the production of aeroplane engines? Australia has done so. I know that her position is different from ours but she has done so. Why has Canada up to the present time not done so? I know what the answer was a year ago or a year and a half ago. It was that it would1 take two years to build up and expand such an industry. But I remember that in 1940, over three years ago, the minister informed the members of this house that it was the intention of the government to canvass the situation with respect to the production of aeroplane engines in Canada, and he indicated at the same time that he expected that the production of aeroplane engines would be proceeded with in this country. I appreciate the explanation which the minister has given, but it is only in this way, by the asking of questions and by frank statements from the minister, that many things

War Appropriation-Supplies
which appear incomprehensible without explanation are explained1 to the satisfaction not only of the members of the house but of the country.
One thing more. When I mentioned the other day that there was a reduction of Canadian production within a year of from about 400 planes a month to 320 a month at the present time, and that the same nine models are still being produced that were being produced then, the minister made a statement as to which I should like a further explanation. He said, as reported in Hansard, at page 3606:
May I say to my hon. friend that there would be forty times the number of man-hours in the production of a Lancaster bomber than there would be in the production of a Fleet trainer. That is the reason for the smaller number of planes. But the tonnage of planes goes steadily higher.
If we take that statement at its face value, it means this, that Canada's production in tonnage increases year by year. Would the minister furnish the committee with information showing the tonnage of planes produced in 1941, 1942, and 1943 to date?
If I may be allowed, I will look over some of the questions I asked the other day to ascertain whether or not-
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have a short memory. Why not let me take these in small batches?
Very well.

My hon. friend asks why we do not increase the production of aeroplanes. I was trying to explain that we are increasing the production, and working very hard at it. We shall still have to find quite a few thousand men for our aeroplane plants to bring ourselves up to our present objective.
Are you short of men at the present time?
Certainly we are short of men.
To what extent?

Well, we are adding men to our aeroplane plants. As my hon. friend knows, we are trying to cut down less essential parts of the programme and divert men to aeroplane plants. I cannot say how many we are short, but I can say that any man who has any skill at all that is useful in an aeroplane plant will be hired if he goes to the gates.
Are the Department of Labour still calling men out of aeroplane plants?
For the armed services?
For service.
For service overseas?
No; for the armed services in Canada.
Certainly they are.
For the draft?

Certainly they are. I said a while ago that the time had come in our programme when the Department of Munitions and Supply were going to ask for no exemptions from the armed services and that is the situation except in respect of men with very unusual skills. When we had to have men; when we were building up from very small beginnings, there were men whom we regarded as essential. To-day the industry is large enough that we do not regard any individual as essential unless he has a very special technical skill.
My hon. friend points out that the programme of aeroplanes in the United States is twenty-five per cent of the total programme, and he asks why ours is not twenty-five per cent.
No; I asked why is it not increased.

Well, it is about twenty-five per cent. Does my hon. friend realize that we have a billion dollars of orders on our books for aeroplanes which we are called upon to deliver about July or August next year?
Yes; but it is not a quarter of this year's expenditures.
One billion dollars.
It is for the two years.

No, no. We have to-day standing on our books unfilled orders to the extent of a billion dollars, and our programme calls for these orders to be filled within twelve months from now-which is a full quarter of our expected expenditure for the current fiscal year.

But how much was
the expenditure last year?

Well, there is the tooling-up expenditure. We will throw that in, if you like. I do not know how much it was, but we will throw it in, and call it $50,000,000 spent and $950,000,000 to go, anything my hon. friend likes. I am pointing out that the proportion of expenditure on aeroplanes to
War Appropriation-Supplies

the total expenditure is, roughly, twenty-five per cent in this country, just as it is in the United States.
Well, I hope all the reckoning is not as loose as that, that I can take off fifty million dollars.

I can take another fifty million dollars off and it will still be twenty-five per cent. The total expenditure for the current fiscal year is, roughly, three and a half billion dollars, and I am saying- that aeroplanes delivered on that programme will represent about twenty-five per cent of that value. It may be twenty per cent and it may be thirty per cent, but it is roughly twenty-five per cent.
The minister means that that is the objective, anyway.
Yes. In other words, our programme is about the same proportionately as the programme of the United States, in so far as the current fiscal year calls for provision of aeroplanes.
But what was the proportion last year?

I cannot say that. Let us answer one question at a time. We have still several hours to go. Do not shoot questions so fast. The hon. member has four in now. Let him sit down and allow me to answer these four, and then he can ask some more.
I am rising-
I have the floor.

Mr. Chairman, I
am rising to a point of order, even if the minister has the floor, and my point of order is this. I am asking the minister a very courteous question: what is the expenditure-
That is not a point of order.
What was the expenditure last year?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On the point of order, the hon. member for Lake Centre must realize that he has asked many, many questions. It is absolutely impossible for the minister, with the assistance that he has, to answer them all in rotation unless he is allowed the time to do so, without interference. On this point of order I call attention to standing order 41, citation 312 Beauchesne, at page 103:
Whilst a member is addressing the house, no one has a right to interrupt him by putting a question to him, or by making or demanding an. explanation. A member will at times allow such interruptions through a sense of courtesy to another, but it is entirely at the option of the member in possession of the floor to give -way or not to an immediate explanation.

I suggest
that that does not apply when the house is in committee. If the Chairman will read the rules he will know that that refers to when Mr. Speaker is in the Chair.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With due respect to
the hon. member for York-Sunbury, I have read the rules, and I have given my ruling.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The hon. member has no right to cast any reflection on the Chair.

What
county is heard from? If the hon. member wants to say anything, let him rise in his place.

There can be only one member on his feet at a time. If we can preserve that rule I shall be very glad to carry on.
With regard to the hon. member's question, my officers have made a rough calculation and say that for the last two years the production has amounted, roughly, to twenty-five per cent of the total expenditure. What is the next question? I wish I could answer these one at a time.

As to
cargo planes and engines.

As a matter of fact Canada
has not overlooked the building of cargo planes. We have been building the Norseman for the last year. They are coming off the line as fast as we can turn them out, and they are being eagerly taken up not only by this country but by the United States. We expect to be in production of another cargo plane. I do not like to say anything about it; as a matter of fact I have not said anything about it. It is a transoceanic plane which is built wholly for cargo purposes. We have started also the design of a plane which we believe will be the ideal plane for Canada for transport work.

Would
that be something like the Commando or the Curtiss-Wright ?

The Commando is a twin-engined plane and I believe this is a four-engined plane. But it will be a wholly modern transport plane. I ask hon. members to keep in mind that at the present moment this is in the design stage. It must go from the design stage to the complete design stage and then it must go through the production stage. That means that it is two or three years away. Nevertheless we are designing a plane of allCanadian design which we think will be the

War Appropriation-Supplies
plane of the future. It is the first time that Canada has ever undertaken that type of designing job.
Would the minister object to telling the committee where that cargo plane of the type he has just spoken of will be built? If he has any objection to answering I would not want to press it.

Well, I would rather not, if
my hon. friend does not mind. There are reasons why I prefer not to give information about that plane at the moment.
. Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): It has not reached the stage where you have designed, anyway.
The hon. member was speaking of the plant that I was discussing before?
The Norseman.

That is in the Noorduyn plant in Montreal. There is another plane being turned out in another plant which we hope to have coming off the assembly line in September or October of this year. It will be the north Atlantic type of plane. We are starting the design of a plane which will be wholly Canadian, designed and Canadian built. It is well on in the design stage at the moment.
The question was asked why we did not start now with the building of engines. I told the house, perhaps two years ago, that I had obtained an appropriation from the government to undertake the building of aeroplane engines in this country and was investigating the situation. As a matter of fact, I once upon a time obtained an appropriation of $40,000,000 to build a plant for aeroplane engines in Canada. Exhaustive studies were made and we decided on a type of engine that we would build here. The construction of the plant, the training of operatives and the installation of machinery were to cost $40,000,000. We got to the point where it was a question of buying machinery. Machine tools at that time were in very great demand. The United States was not in the war at the time, but the munitions business there was stepping up to that point where they were reluctant to allow any unnecessary drain of machine tool capacity from outside. The Canadian industry was expanding rapidly. There was a tremendous demand for machine tools here. I went to the United States with a request that we be authorized to buy machine tools to the value of $15,000,000-critical tools which were in great demand in that country. I was courteously received, but I was told that it was impossible for the United States to authorize
that expenditure on tools. I pointed out our position at that time. Our source of engines was England and that had been cut off. It was just after Dunkirk and we could not obtain engines from the other side. I said that I must have engines. I was told that we could get our requirements. A few days' production from their assembly lines would meet our needs, and they said they would undertake to give us engines. Canada has never had an areoplane waiting for an engine since that day. The promise has been kept and kept well. Had we built those engines we would have used a great deal of manpower, and. manpower of a skilled type was exceedingly scarce at that time. Indeed, it as no more plentiful to-day than it was then.
The building of engines is an exceedingly intricate job that calls for great care. We could have built engines in Canada, but we would have been building one type of engines whereas we have planes using perhaps fifteen types of^engines. We have changed engines in our planes from time to time. For instance, the Anson plane has been re-engined twice, and *we are now bringing out still a third type of plane which has a third type of engine, each type being of a somewhat higher horse-power. By having a sure supply of engines, we were [DOT] able to choose a particular type of engine that would give the best performance in the planes we built.
We obtain other items from the United States. We obtain the larger type of diesel engine used in their tanks. We could build diesel engines here, but we are satisfied to buy diesel engines from the large output in the United States. If we had undertaken a policy in this war of building every part of every munition we have turned out, we would have built far fewer munitions than we have under the present arrangement. I can also say that we build certain parts of munitions in Canada for which we are sole suppliers to the United States. Even the United States have not thought it necessary to be wholly self-contained in its munitions programme. They are quite willing to depend on Canada for certain components for munitions that are built in the United States.
As regards our future in aviation, the government is not in any way handicapped by the fact that we do not build engines in this country. We have a certain source of supply, and we can go on with confidence and build frames with the knowledge that our engine requirements will be met when the time comes. That is the story of engines.
War Appropriation-Supplies
The day before yesterday I raised two or three questions. The minister has perhaps not yet had time to answer them. Does he care to answer now?
Steel for agricultural implements?
That was the first question.

We have followed fairly well the policy of the United States in meeting the requirements of the agricultural industry, and necessarily so, because we are a deficit country in steel, and a considerable part of our requirements comes from the United States. In 1942 we followed the policy of the United States in supplying twenty-five per cent of the steel for agriculture which was supplied to that industry in 1940. In this year we have also followed the United States in providing eighty-five per cent of the steel for agriculture that was supplied to agriculture in 1940. In other words, in the current year we have increased the steel allocations to agriculture by about 120 per cent.
Would the minister say something about the service stations staying open on Saturday nights?
The present regulations provide that they may stay open until 9 o'clock on Saturday evenings.
That has been passed for this year?

It carries on from last year. The difficulty is that the operators are having a hard time in manning the stations, but the stations that stayed open in the evening last year have the continuing right to stay open this year. The privilege has never been cancelled. and the same stations can do so. There has been no great demand for an extension of the time to 10 p.m. I have discussed the matter with the oil controller, and he says that if there were a large demand for an extension of an hour he would not have any great objection, but he himself had never received that request.
There was a third question about the reclamation of used lubricating oil.

That does not come within my province. The Department of Munitions and Supply supplies the requirements of the armed services. We supply whatever the armed services requisition, but salvage is a matter for the armed services. Waste lubricants belong to the army, the navy or the air force, as the case may be, and they are

entitled to make their own arrangements for salvage. I understand that the army have reclaiming plants.

I have tried all day to get the eye of the chairman and I have only now succeeded. May I say, first of all, that there seems to have been a misunderstanding as to how this discussion should be carried on. We agreed after the Minister of Finance had made his statement and presented his budget to take up the different services. The ministers of the different departments, we understood, would come on and we would have a general discussion; then we would go into each particular item, and the discussion would then be confined to that item. I thought that was still the understanding when we began this discussion after the minister made his statement last Friday, but we seem to have been jumping all over the map. I can only hope that this will facilitate getting through these items as we come to deal with them, which I expect will be within a few minutes after this first item is passed.
When the house adjourned late yesterday afternoon we had spent practically the whole sitting on the question of rubber, and I thought almost everything had been said that could or should be said. But when we started in again this afternoon the question of rubber came up again, and except for the times when the minister was endeavouring to answer some of the questions asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre we devoted most of the afternoon to the same subject. The only additional contributions that we got this afternoon, as compared with what was brought up yesterday, was the statement that the minister is going to see that investigations are continued into the production of synthetic rubber from alcohol produced from wheat. I think he also agreed that if in their experiments they find a greater possibility than is apparent now that rubber may be produced in this way, then the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, which I think I mentioned myself yesterday as well, will be accepted and the industry will be commenced in western Canada where the raw products are produced. I think those were the only two matters of any consequence that came up this afternoon in addition to what was said yesterday.
On Friday last the minister reviewed the work of his department for the past three years, then dealt with the present, and in these estimates is providing for the future. He dealt with the matter from those three aspects. I find that during his statement he mentioned in detail some twenty articles or commodities

War Appropriation-Supplies
produced under the supervision of his departs raent. During the discussion yesterday and to-day, I think we have touched upon half of those commodities; so that, as I said before,
I hope that when we come to deal with the specific items the discussion we have had already will facilitate their adoption. The one point which I believe should be' kept in mind is the fact that we started practically from, scratch in 1939; that was the thought expressed yesterday by the hon. member for Yale. Having that in mind, and looking at the information we have been given as to what has been done since then, I think to be fair we must say that a great deal has been accomplished.; I was going to say that the department had done wonders. Of course we must consider also the cost of all this, including the assistance given to industry. I believe the minister was quite frank in that regard and in answering the questions which we asked along that line.
Following the statement made yesterday by the hon. member for Yale, I was impressed also by the statement given by the minister's assistant, the hon. member for Stormont. I think a precedent was established, on that occasion. The hon. gentleman outlined to this committee how the whole organization has been set up; how it carries on; how it controls the cost and the price of various commodities, and so on. I believe the minister made the statement that by means of this organization, imperfect though it may have been, a saving of $155,000,000 has been made, and I have no doubt that is correct. I think the minister is entitled to a great deal of credit in that respect. Then the hon. member for Stormont went on to deal with the question of control, and in dealing with the question of auditors said that they had men in the various branches who were capable of properly appraising the value of the component parts going into any article produced. If that policy is continued they cannot but do good work.
Then the hon. member dealt rwith the question of contracts, how they are let and how they are controlled'. I think he divided them into two classes. The first class to which he referred he called contractors who are costconscious, which I would interpret to mean in plain English contractors who are honest.
No, Mr. Chairman, that is not fair. By "cost-conscious" we mean contractors who are always looking for a chance to reduce the cost, who keep an open mind and try to improve the methods used.
That is honesty, is it not?
But a contractor who takes a job and does it as the manual calls for it to be done is also honest. Perhaps he has not as much inventive genius.

Perhaps the minister and I are saying the same thing in different ways, but I say that a contractor who appreciates that it is his responsibility and duty to endeavour to produce the article at the lowest cost possible is making a contribution to our war effort. In that connection I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West made a splendid statement this afternoon in which he did credit to himself and to Consolidated Smelters plant at Trail, when he dealt with the cost of the commodity being produced there.
Then the hon. member for Stormont referred to the other class of contractor and went on at some length to discuss the difficulties that have been experienced at times with respect to some of these contractors, showing how they are controlled and so on. In my opinion the hon. member gave a splendid outline of those items which enter into the question of cost and those other items which, practically speaking, do not. I think the precedent established was good, and I believe that if the other departments had followed the same practice, hon. members would have obtained a great deal of information which would have obviated much of the discussion that took place in connection with the three departments with which we have dealt. Then I believe the leader of the opposition made a valuable contribution the other evening when he made a plea for consideration for labour and the little man, as he termed him. If labour and agriculture get the proper consideration in connection with this industrial programme, I think it will go a long way to preserve our democracy, and I hope the minister will take that into consideration. I do not believe any group of people should have the control that we are led to believe some of them have.
Hon. members who have spoken already have reviewed the minister's statement in some detail and in turn have asked for information to which the committee was entitled and which I think the minister gave as fully as possible. Some hon. members have made constructive suggestions, and it is only right that they should do so. On two or three occasions the hon. member for Lake Centre has made a worth-while contribution to the debate when he has asked for certain information. Some of that information he has received and some of the replies may not

War Appropriation-Supplies
have satisfied him. The fact remains, however, that we now have information we did not have before.
The hon. member for Lake Centre dealt with assistance which had been given to industry, the establishing of industry, and conditions in the post-war period. He concluded his speech of a few days ago by offering four constructive suggestions, and hon. members will find them at page 3605 of Hansard.. It will be found that he referred to a plan for the demobilization of industries, and outlined what might be done with some industries in the' post-war period.
His first suggestion was that there should be a determination of the basis upon which sale or disposition should be made. That recommendation has been covered to a certain extent by the minister, and we hope it may be enlarged upon still farther. He recommended, in the second place, that there be a government plan now for the conversion of war-time industries to peace-time economy and production. His third recommendation was that there should be a determination now as to which plants will be continued after the war for stand-by purposes. His last recommendation was that there be a plan of assistance to small industries after the war by way of loans, to stimulate the change from the war-time to peace-time economy, coupled with technical advice as to the most appropriate use of their facilities in peace-time production.
I believe, if the last recommendation in particular, is considered, some of these industries would be placed in western Canada. One might refer particularly to the implement industry. Surely implements should be produced in western Canada, where they would be needed, and facilities could be set up for refitting or repairing many of the implements which to-day are standing idle. Possibly some of those implements are idle on account of a lack of man-power, but the fact remains that they are not being used owing to the circumstances under which farmers are being forced to farm.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made a commendable contribution to the debate when he dealt with the aluminum company, and the power development at Shipshaw. I shall not discuss that matter in detail, because when we are considering the item we shall no doubt hear more from the hon. members concerned and the minister.
Listening to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and some other hon. members, I have been disturbed when I have thought of the stranglehold that some of these large industries have upon Canada's resources, and the

control they exercise in respect of the development of those resources. This should be dealt with, and in such a way that we shall not lose control.
The hon. member for Davenport has spoken several times about the production of oil from tar sands. I think however, that on the last occasion he spoke he made an exceptionally clear presentation of the subject so much so, in fact, that I believe he impressed the minister. I should hope that the minister might consider carefully the facts presented by the hon. member for Davenport, and that as a result we might see a development in the -processing of these sands. The minister pointed out last night that certain ingredients might be removed from the crude oil, but that the quantity of gasoline produced would not be lessened. It would seem, therefore, that careful consideration should be given to the development of these tar sands. One might visualize a great development in this respect in the reconstruction period. I need only add that I am sure agriculturists will do their part and make a worth-while contribution when called upon to do so.
I should like to refer for a few moments to a matter I brought to the attention of the house last Monday, namely, the invention of a new carburettor by Melford J. Ball of Wey-burn, Saskatchewan. I refer to the matter now because I do not think I was given the opportunity I should have had on Monday to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. I believe that in speaking when the orders of the day were called I was in order. However, as I was then ruled out of order, I shall place the facts before the minister this evening.
This young man from Weyburn has invented a carburettor. The invention has been tried out on standard models of cars, and has had the result of increasing their gasoline mileage by over fifty per cent. Associated with Mr. Ball is a young man named Lewis Jacques of Edinburgh. Mr. Jacques is a master mechanic attached to the Royal Air Force stationed at Weyburn. This young man says that Ball has something definitely worth while, and something which should be investigated by the government. Mr. Ball only asks that he be given an opportunity of proving that he has a satisfactory invention. He is prepared to give it over to the government, or to any branch of the service, if it will be used to reduce the gasoline consumption not only of the general public but of the different services, in their buses, trucks and other vehicles.

War Appropriation-Supplies
If this man has a worth-while invention, then certainly it should be investigated at once. If it is a good carburettor, the government should have a man try it out. I should not like this invention to suffer the same fate as was suffered by the Pogue carburettor. I happen to know quite a bit about that carburettor, because a close friend of mine had something to do with financing Pogue when he was working on his invention. I know what happened to that carburettor, and I think the minister probably knows, too. I am not going to put that on record, but I know we do not hear much about Pogue to-day. The big interests have obtained control of that carburettor; we know that. I learned that from a man who is so close to me that I can have no question about it. I refer to the man who helped to finance Pogue. He knows what happened to it. I trust the minister will give this matter some consideration and have someone make an investigation. If it is worth while, then let us use it and save millions of dollars we would otherwise spend on gasoline.
I trust that we may make more progress in the next day than we have made in the last two. I have not taken much time of the committee; in fact, I have taken only about ten minutes.

I would ask a question in
respect of item 1 which deals with additions and extensions to plants. A large sum of money is involved. Would the minister give a break-down? How much has gone into the extension of government-operated plants as against privately owned plants? I would presume that when funds are provided for the extension of plants, it would be intended that they should be operated as soon as they are ready for operation. I believe funds were provided last year by the government to extend the blast furnace facilities at the Sydney steel plant. I have received a telegram from the steel workers' union in Sydney stating that this new unit has not been put into operation, necessitating a greater use of scrap by the open-hearth furnaces, thus decreasing production, wages and so on. I understood that when funds were made available for the erection of this blast furnace it was the intention that it would be put into operation when completed, but there seems to be some holdup. The steel is needed, and I was wondering if the minister could explain why this new unit is not in operation.

The hon. member asked for a break-down of the item. This will be found at pages 3698 and 3699 of Hansard, where this is given in some detail. A loan of $3,507,024.50
was made by the government to the Sydney-steel plant for a blast furnace and other things. I cannot understand why the furnace is not in operation, and I feel quite sure that there is some part or some auxiliary equipment which has not been finished. It is badly needed because we want to put the plate mill on a three-shift basis. I had thought the furnace was in operation and I am interested in hearing that it is not. I shall make inquiry to see what is the present position.

Will the minister explain the present fuel-wood policy of the government? He did not go into that in any detail when he made his statement on June 11. The1 minister is reported at page 3552 of Hansard as saying:
Following the announcement in March that the government would pay fuel-wood dealers a subsidy of $1 per cord, some increase in production has been noted. The situation is still serious, however, and many communities may be in short supply next winter unless immediate, local action is taken.
I judged from that statement that the minister was leaving the burden of this problem with the local authorities. If that is the government policy I fear that many communities will be short of fuel wood in the coming winter. I notice in the new volume of orders in council which we received to-day, No. 10, dated June 14, 1943, there is P.C.4669 which authorizes the wood fuel controller- this control has been set up since the debate on fuel which occurred in this house on March 16-to divert equipment for the production of wood and to make persons who are in a position to do so, produce wood. It also gives him power to purchase and to transport and dispose of wood fuel. It sets out that $1,000,000 has been provided for these purposes. Apparently there has been a change in policy; it would look as though the government is going into the business of producing wood. On May 17 the Minister of Labour stated in the house that he hoped Italian prisoners would be available for the production of wood fuel. There has been mentioned in the press that conscientious objectors are to be used for this purpose; and an order in council has been tabled which gives power to the government to use Japanese in British Columbia for the production of wood fuel. Could the minister give us the exact position at the present time? It will be important to many communities in Canada to know just what help they are going to get from the government in meeting this problem.

The situation is unchanged. My first statement covers the situation to date. The production of wood fuel is a local
War Appropriation-Supplies

problem. In my first statement I offered an active working partnership between the federal government and local communities to assist in meeting fuel requirements. Those local communities that take their obligations seriously and make every effort to solve their own wood fuel problem will have the best time next winter.
It is easier for some communities to do that than others.

That is true. The dominion government is arranging for certain wood fuel operations, and we hope to build up a considerable stock of fuel which may be moved into distress areas next year. This will be simply a safety valve. It will be impossible to promise or even to suggest that any community that does not take an active interest in solving this problem will get wood fuel shipped to it by the dominion government. We are arranging for the cutting of as much wood fuel as we can, and this will be stored where it can be shipped into distress areas.
Is it the intention to use Japanese for that purpose?

We are using anyone we can get. We are using Japanese in British Columbia, but I do not know with what success. We have planned operations for them in the areas where they are at the present time. We have even brought pressure to bear upon ' certain pulp companies to have them start wood fuel operations before they start their winter cutting. We are doing all we can to get supplies of wood fuel. We must always remember that we are not at all sure that we shall have sufficient coal next winter. In fact, I doubt very much if we shall. Therefore, we are attempting to cut wood fuel with the thought in mind that it will help to take up any shortage there may be in coal.
Will the government move this wood to the different centres, or will the consumers have to pay for the cost of moving it?	[DOT]
We will use it to relieve distress if there is distress. We will move the wood.
To the different centres?
Yes; to the dealers.
Could it not be arranged to have the municipal authorities supervise the distribution of the wood in the various centres?

I should not like my hon. friend to suggest that any municipality will

be discharging its obligations if it considers that all it has to do is to supervise the distribution of wood sent in by the federal government. Every municipality must organize efforts to supply wood to the utmost of its ability.
I think the municipalities are doing so.

I think they are. We are helping them with equipment and1 anything else we can. As I say, we are attempting to accumulate considerable stocks of fuel wood at different points in Canada. We are doing this as a protection against the serious situation which we believe is arising. If we cannot get sufficient coal, we will move wood into areas where the situation is serious. But this is simply a reserve that is being built up, and no community should make its plans in the sure belief that wood will be shipped into it next winter.
Is the government still paying the subsidy of $1 a cord?
Yes. I hope to make a statement about the bonus to-morrow. I announced before that the time would be extended, but I have not given the new time limit. I shall try to do that to-morrow.

Is it the intention to build up reserves of fuel wood at certain places and then, if circumstances become sufficiently serious in certain municipalities, those reserves of fuel wood will be shipped in to where there is a shortage?
That is it, yes.

It was my privilege to accompany a delegation of members who recently visited Buffalo and inspected the plants of the Curtiss-Wright corporation. Anyone who was on that trip would agree that it was an inspiration to see the aeroplanes on the assembly line in process of construction. One of the most outstanding features one noticed was how much of the modern aeroplane consists of aluminum. As one stood at the end of the assembly line and looked hundreds of yards down the line where the aeroplanes are first assembled, the general thought was, I believe: If only Hitler could see this! One of our members expressed it as well, I think, as it could be expressed when he said: Thank God, these people are our allies!
During the course of our visit I asked one of the executives of the company of any of the aluminum which was going into the manufacture of these planes came from Canada, and his reply was, "I do not know what we

War Appropriation-Supplies
should do without the aluminum which comes from Arvida and the aluminum castings which come from Kingston." Even if there are certain people in this country who do not appreciate what the Aluminum Company of Canada has done, certainly no one who has gone through these plants and has seen what our United States allies are doing in the production of aeroplanes, can fail to realize just how much the Aluminum company has done not only for our own country but for the united nations as well. In reply to the clamour and consternation that falls on the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation camp whenever private enterprise makes a great contribution not only to Canada's war effort but to that of all our allies, I can only repeat what has already been said in this house, that we are not fighting monopolies; we are fighting a war. I have no more tolerance for monopolies than have my friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, but I believe that this is no time to investigate and interfere with the turning out of a product as cheaply and in such large quantities as Aluminum Company of Canada is turning out this vital product.
I do resent one thing, which I think has not been brought out in this debate, but which I believe should have been brought out, namely, the insinuations that have been made against Canada's minister to Washington, the Hon. Leighton McCarthy. It is my privilege to have known the Hon. Leighton McCarthy for a great many years. I have known him as one of Canada's most successful lawyers and as a great business executive. I have known him as a great philanthropist, and now I can appreciate him as a great diplomat. I think it ill behooves anyone at a time like this deliberately to make insinuations against a man of his ca'ibre occupying the high position he does. I know of no surer way to drive men of his type, the very highest type, out of public and diplomatic life in this country. It is my opinion, and the opinion of a great many others, that what the Aluminum company has done so far in this war will rank as one of the great production achievements in this struggle.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The other evening the hon. member for Yale asked some questions in connection with construction contracts generally, and I should like to make an answer to him at this time. If the hon. member will look at what was said the day before yesterday on the subject of contracts, he will see that the statement was made that contracts generally may be divided under two heads, fixed price contracts and contracts of a cost-plus nature, and that four-sevenths, in point of number, of the contracts let were, 72537-238
generally speaking, let on a fixed .price basis, and that applies to construction contracts as well. They are let on a competitive basis by tender, and I think it is safe to say that from seventy-five to eighty per cent of those contracts have been let by tender. Exceptional circumstances, however, sometimes make it impossible to let contracts on that basis, and then the contract is let on a cost plus a fixed fee basis.
With reference to the specific case in which the hon. member was concerned, the military camp at Vernon, the contract was let on a cost plus a fixed fee basis.
Are you getting away from cost-plus contracts?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Yes, definitely. The
number of cost-plus contracts is continually being reduced.
They should be wiped out entirely.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
It is hoped that they will be wiped out entirely in favour of the fixed price contract, but in this case there was a reason for the exceptional basis. This is the reason.
In 1942 there was an unprecedented request for different defence projects on the west coast, and this coupled with the activities of the United - States government on the Alaska military highway and the facilities required in connection with it, made it impossible for the Department of Munitions and Supply or anybody else to obtain competitive tenders.
The contractors were unable to maintain their men on account of the high rates paid on the Alaska military highway. The supplies of material became restricted. Priorities on materials required from the United States became difficult to obtain, and lastly,, transportation facilities, particularly to outlying points, were at such a premium that the contractors refused under the combination of circumstances to submit firm price tenders.
It therefore became necessary, in order to meet the demands of the armed services for defence projects, that the work required be placed under way as early as possible and in such a manner as would assure its completion at as early a date as possible.
The director of construction in this case examined the capabilities of the different contractors in the district with regard to their being immediately available, also as to their supply of plant and equipment, the type of their organization, their location and the materials at their command, and selected

War Appropriation-Supplies

Messrs. Bennett and White of Calgary as the most suitable and arrangements were made with them to undertake the work.
The hon. member also asked who was included in the fixed fee; what profit there was. I am informed that the fixed fee covers the following items: (a) the services of the partners of the firm or directors of the company, ail of which are available at no charge to the contract; Ob) all head office expenses; (c) all costs of financing; (d) all other expenses other than those which are directly incurred on the site of the work; (e) the services of all employees at head office for the use of purchasing, expediting, engineering or the giving of any service ordinarily handled in head office; (f) as the fee is ordinarily set at $25,000 for a million dollars worth of work and all the above services have to be provided out of this fee, it is clearly evident that the amount of .profit is unduly small. As a matter of fact, the contractors in this case have complained that by reason of slowness of payment their financing charges have absorbed practically the whole of the fee. The profit is therefore very small.

There is one item I should
like to bring to the minister's attention. It may be that we have to leave these matters until a later hour because we are located so far from the Chair.
I do not know to what degree the minister is responsible for the disposition of the various types of commodities for the production of which he is responsible. The matter I wish to bring to his attention is in connection with gasoline, namely, the fact that it appears from correspondence which I have received that there is a great deal of dissatisfaction with respect to the uses made of army vehicles for civilian purposes-if I may put it in that way -or for private purposes.

We have nothing to do with
that. The army file requests with us and we fill those requests in full. The distribution of gasoline or the use to which it is put is wholly a matter for the army.

Just one point, then. May
I indicate to the minister that he might have less difficulty in providing the gasoline requirements for the army and for civilian purposes if he would bring to the attention of the Minister of National Defence that there is, according to a number of documents which I have, colossal waste, as they state, in the use of gasoline, by virtue of the fact that it is evident to anyone who is in centres where military camps are located that these army vehicles are being used for other than

army purposes. I will not elaborate on that now, since the minister has already indicated that it is not his responsibility, but I could produce some interesting evidence in that direction which has come to me. I would ask him to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of National Defence.

I wonder if we could direct attention
particularly to item 1. A very wide discussion has been allowed up to the present, and I have noted that rubber has bounced back more than once-which is of course the usual thing with rubber-but I wonder if we could come to item 1 and get it carried.

The
agenda which has been given to us does not cover many of these items we have been discussing. There was no particular place to discuss synthetic rubber unless it be in these items. I should like to know under what item I could ask a question about gasoline and the oil controller's department?
Departmental administration.

I
wish to put to the minister one question which has been asked of me by two manufacturers. Has he any idea how many civilians in munitions plants it takes to sustain one man in the armed forces? These manufacturers asked that because they are trying to keep up the morale of the men in their plants.

I cannot say. We have at
the present time well over seven hundred thousand men in the services. We have close to a million men and women in war production. I assume we have more than two millions in agriculture and civilian industries. That would represent about four to one, would it not? I never saw a figure on that, and I doubt whether any arbitrary figure can be given.

The
minister has not the figure?

No; I have no figure about
that. I gave the population distribution as well as I could. I do not think there is any known ratio. It depends upon a good many factors. It would be pretty difficult, I think, to work that out.

The
reason why these men wanted to know is that when they are talking to the men in the plants, telling them that they want to get this production, they wish to be able to say that "it takes ten, or forty, or a hundred of you men and women to keep one man in the

War Appropriation-Supplies
armed forces, and if one of you lays off on a Saturday or a Sunday or a Monday, it means that a man in the armed forces is handicapped that much."
