I should like to be able to give my hon. friend a figure, but I do not know that any study has been made. Perhaps I could have one made and give him the result in two or three weeks.

I
believe it would help the manufacturers in that it would stimulate the munitions workers.

One'word on this item concerning Victory Aircraft. As one of those who have been critical constantly, and I think from what the minister said to-night, with great justification, of the set-up at Malton, I had an opportunity this week of visiting the plant, and in my opinion the management there now is endeavouring to do and, I believe, will succeed in doing a thoroughly capable job of producing Lancaster bombers. Probably they have a little overestimated their capacity. But I am glad to see that the present manager has been maintained by the department. I think he deserves every support because he certainly has had a great deal to try him. For years this plant has gone through frightful vicissitudes and difficulties. I was glad to hear the minister's statement to that effect.
One thing more. I have heard it stated that if the minister will use his great efforts and forceful drive to see that the Weston cut-off is paved for the two or three miles from No. 10 highway into Weston, it will be equivalent in the saving of wear and tear on cars to two Lancaster bombers from now to the end of the year.

Will the minister explain to the committee the assistance which has been given in the Steep Rock iron development in lake Superior district? Apparently the government has given assistance of one kind and another to that development, and it would be interesting to know the nature and extent, and also when it is expected that the mine will be in production, whether the iron ore which is produced is to be all smelted and used in Canada, or whether there is any provision that a certain proportion of it must be smelted and used in Canada.

The government cooperated with the Canadian National Railways in setting rates for transportation which would be competitive with rates from the Mesaba area. The management reached an impasse with the
72537-238i
railway in arriving at that rate. There is a certain rate from Mesaba range to lake Superior covering transportation from the mine and loading on to vessels. The mileage from Steep Rock area is longer and the volume of traffic less intensive, with the result that the railway thought it could not justify itself in quoting a competitive rate. The difference was twenty cents a ton for the ore transported. The government arranged to support the transportation by a bonus of twenty cents a ton payable to the railway on the first five million tons moved from the mine to the lakehead. The railway undertook to build the necessary ore dock to tranship the ore from rail to boat, and the government undertook to lend the money to the railway for that purpose, the loan to be recoverable by an amortization charge sufficient to pay interest on amortization of the amount.
How much does that involve altogether?
The subsidy is $1,000,000-twenty cents a ton on five million tons. The cost of the trackage at both ends, and the ore dock, will be around $2,500,000.
What about the other questions? When will the mine be in production?

I do not know when the mine will be in production. We have nothing to do with anything except transportation from the mine. The only place in which the government has intervened is in the. matter of transportation, which we undertook to make competitive with the Mesaba ore. The building of the development is a wholly private enterprise in which the government is not interested in any way.

Apparently that was a new venture in government policy. A press release from the minister's department, dated September 30 of last year, after an announcement about the facilities to be built, contains these words:
Mr. Howe announced that the policy of assistance was decided upon as a result of a decision of the war committee of the cabinet that the development of Steep Rock iron ore deposits should be proceeded with as a means of protecting Canada against a possible shortage of iron ore to meet wTar requirements.
If that is correct, it clearly shows that this was government policy and that the government is very much interested in the development. I believe that this spring there were press reports to the effect that production was expected in about a year and a half. Can the minister say whether or not those statements were correct?
War Appropriation-Supplies

I cannot say. I do not think any member of the government could say. Transportation comes after the development is completed. If the development is successful, we are obligated to furnish certain transportation, which we will do; but in the meantime we expect the mine management to advise us when the property will be ready for transportation facilities. They have not done so as yet, and I really do not know how they are getting along. As I understand the problem, in the first place the power plant must be moved and the Seine river diverted, then the Steep Rock lake pumped out, and after that they are in a positon to undertake mining development. I may be very willing to give forecasts, but I am not willing to state the time that will elapse in an operation of that kind over which I have no control.
But this is war policy, according to the minister's own department. Obviously, assistance is being given to help Canada's war production.
Its possible war needs.
Does the minister mean that no steps were taken to find out the approximate time it would take for this mine to come into production? I did not ask for the exact time.

We have the engineers' report. They were estimating that two years would be taken. That may or may not be optimistic, but I have no control over the operation and I do not see why I should be asked to give an estimate. I have given the engineers' estimate and that is the best I can do.
If the minister had given that before, it would have saved a lot of time. Two years from last fall?
Yes.

I asked the minister whether or not there was any obligation on the company to have this iron ore smelted in Canada or to have it used in Canada. They are getting 83,500,000 assistance from the Canadian government. Is there any understanding with regard to where that iron ore is to be smelted and used?
I am told that the Canadian mills will have first call on the output. The underwriting agreement provides for that.
Is that in the shape of an agreement with the government?
No; the agreement with the underwriters.
The government has no agreement in writing with the company?
No.

The underwriters were a firm, Otis and Company, in Cleveland, and the United States government. The Reconstruction Finance Corporation put up $5,000,000, and Cyrus Eaton and his associates in Cleveland put up the rest of the money to finance it immediately.
This government did not interest itself in the financing of the project.
That is the point I am trying to get at. The dominion government took no part in financing Steep Rock?
No.
The only thing it did was to provide subventions to the Canadian National Railways and build the ore dock.
Well, the ore dock is an obligation of the railway as part of the transportation.
And that is included-

The only assistance given by the Canadian government was assistance to the Canadian National Railways, to put the Canadian National Railways in a position to give a competitive transportation rate to Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited. Our only agreement is with Canadian National Railways.
I have been rather critical of the deal by reason of the fact that we allowed the development to be financed outside Canada.
Has the minister's department interested itself at all in the stock manipulations that have taken place in connection with that property-
Not at all.
-on the strength of the help the government has given?
No.
That is being used for stock manipulations.

The government has given absolutely no help to Steep Rock mines. The only agreement the government has is with Canadian National Railways. Canadian National Railways have quoted a certain rate to Steep Rock mines to transport ore from the mine and put it on board the boat at the lakehead. That is the only agreement there is between any government agency and Steep Rock mine. How the capital was raised,

War Appropriation-Supplies
I have no knowledge and the government has no knowledge, and I wish to make it clear that if there was manipulation, based on the government's interest in the actual construction, we have none. Our only obligation comes after construction has been completed and the mine is in production. If ore comes out, it is our obligation to transport it from the mine to lakehead and put it on the boat at a certain over-all rate.

What was the
arrangement for the building of the dock?

The dock will be built and owned by the Canadian National Railways, to whom the government will loan the money required for that purpose. The Canadian National Railways will pay the government six cents on every ton of ore passing over that dock for interest and amortization, until the government loan is fully amortized.

I should like to ask a question in regard to the Cherrier plant in Quebec which is operated on a management fee basis by Canada Car and Munitions Limited. I wish to know whether or not the magazine entitled "Employees' Cherrier House Organ" is paid for by the government, directly or indirectly. A recent issue of this magazine, which is put out by that plant, contains a most disruptive statement, which I need not place before the committee. I should like to know whether the government makes payment in any degree for that magazine, and I suggest to the government that there be an investigation into some of the statements made therein, to the end that these statements be excluded from further issues.

I have never seen the publication in question, but my financial adviser tells me that expenditures of that kind are not permitted as an element of cost, so that I presume it does not enter into the cost. However, I shall be glad to make inquiries about the publication about which, as a matter of fact, I have never heard.

Despite the fact that the subject of aluminum has been introduced once or twice to-day, I do not intend to continue that discussion to-night. I should like to direct one question to the minister, or perhaps to his assistant. The hon. member for Stormont speaking on Tuesday last, as reported at page 3648 of Hansard, said:
Under existing tax laws no corporation can earn, after tax, a greater amount than seventy per cent of its pre-war standard profit.
As the minister knows, and as is borne out on page 10 of the prospectus of the Aluminum Company of Canada and on pages 11 and 14 of the report of Aluminium Limited, these
interests in 1942 were making profits greater than in previous years; in fact, as far as Aluminium Limited is concerned they were the greatest in its history. I wonder if either the minister or bis assistant would reconcile these facts with the statement to which I have referred.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that the earnings of the Aluminum Company of Canada this year had been the greatest in its history?

I said that the earnings of both the Aluminum Company of Canada and Aluminium Limited were larger in 1942 than in the pre-war years, and in the case of Aluminium Limited the largest in its history. There was one year, 1939, when the Aluminum Company of Canada made, perhaps 8100,000 more than in 1942, but if you take the average of the pre-war years it is considerably lower than the profit in 1942.
Yes; but the volume and the facilities had t>een multiplied several times by then.

But I am comparing this situation with the statement by the assistant to the minister, which was to the effect that no corporation can earn, after tax, a greater amount than 70 per cent of its pre-war standard profit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The statement to which the hon. gentleman refers was made by me on June 15. At the time I was going on to refer to the checks and controls that we exercised in the Department of Munitions and Supply over contracts of a cost-plus nature. I went on to explain that over and above that there were under the jurisdiction of the Department of Finance the corporation tax and the excess profits tax, and the figures I mentioned on that occasion were the figures given by the Minister of Finance in his 1942 budget. I made a further statement saying that no change had been made this year. Now the hon. gentleman asks a question in connection with these aluminum companies and wants an explanation. I have not seen the figures to which he refers and, of course, I cannot explain them, other than the statement I now make.
Mr. NOSEtyORTHY: Is it not a fact that the basis is not the total amount of the profits but the percentage of the turnover?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That is a matter for the Department of Finance, not for Munitions and Supply.

Item agreed to.
War Appropriation-Supplies
2. Cargo vessels-Operated by Park Steamship Limited, $45,000,000

Would the minister be good enough to give the committee some information with regard to the companies which have chartered vessels from the Park Steamship Company? As reported at page 3550 of Hansard I note that the minister said:
Up to the present time twelve vessels of 10,000 tons deadweight; five vessels of 4,700 tons deadweight, and one tanker have been delivered to the company.
It is important, I believe, that the committee be informed as to what steamship companies have chartered these cargo vessels, and I should like to know how many are operating on the Atlantic and how many on the Pacific.

I am sorry to say I have not that list at hand, though I will have it at three o'clock to-morrow. It changes from trip to trip. The boats are allocated to various trades by the Canada shipping board, and a ship is chartered to a particular company operating in the trade to which the boat has been allocated. For instance, if the boat has been allocated to the United Kingdom trade, it would be chartered to Cunard, White Star, the Donaldson line, or the Canadian Pacific. If it were operating to Australia, it would be chartered to the Canadian-Australasian line or some other line that in the past has operated to Australia.
Do the steamship companies which charter these vessels pay a set fee based on the cost of the vessel, or how is the charter fee arrived at?

The ship is operated for the account of Park Steamship company, and the full returns are made to that company less the amount of the fee retained by the operating company, which is at the rate of $3,500 per annum plus two and a half per cent of the value of the cargo.
Is the same arrangement entered into with regard to financial payments?
No; we charter ships to the British ministry of war transport for a dollar a year. What arrangements the British ministry of war transport make for their own account, I cannot say.
How many of the ships turned over to the Park Steamship company are of Canadian register, or are they all of Canadian register?
They are all of Canadian register.

I should like to say a few words in connection with wage rates on those boats. The minister may have forgotten, but I wrote him in August, 1942, on this point. There is considerable complaint respecting the wage scales for both officers and men. I understand the scale in effect on Canadian ships is the British scale of wages.
For officers.
For officers and men.
No; it is higher for men.

I have the minister's letter of September 17, 1942, and I find this sentence in it:
The wage scale in effect on these vessels corresponds to that on vessels operated on the Atlantic coast under the supervision of the Park Steamship Company, and is in exact conformity with the wage rates of the British national maritime board.
Then the minister goes on to say :
I quite concur in the company's opinion that it would be unwise to operate vessels out of Pacific ports with a wage rate at variance with that of vessels operated by the same company out of Atlantic ports.
It is a matter of fact that wage rates on the Pacific coast have always been higher than those on the Atlantic coast and, generally speaking wage rates on Canadian boats, and more particularly on United States boats, are much higher than wage rates on British boats. I have had considerable correspondence on this matter with the Canadian seamen's union, British Columbia section, and the Canadian merchant service guild, officers' organization. They have been good enough to forward me copies of all the correspondence which passed between themselves and the manager for the Park Steamship company, whom I believe to be Mr. R. B. Teakle. I find there is considerable dissatisfaction with the rates of pay.
In a letter dated September 14, 1942, replying to a letter from Mr. Teakle the officers of the Canadian merchant guild write as follows:
This guild is very disappointed with the attitude taken by your company on the above question. First, our information is, and we believe it to be authentic, that more than the two vessels you mentioned will be for Canadian register.
Mr. Teakle, in his letter to the guild, said there would be only two of these vessels under Canadian register. The letter continues:
Secondly, in regard to these ships being fully manned we believe this is correct, due in some

War Appropriation-Supplies
measure, in so far as masters and deck officers are concerned to this organization's attitude, as in nearly every instance we were consulted by the officers who were offered the positions for advice on the advisability of signing on, when we advised these officers that it was not in the policy of this guild to interfere in the manning of these ships, regardless of the scales of pay or other conditions, as we consider this service part of our war effort, and we had, on September 7, 1939, written the then Minister of National Defence, the Hon. Ian Mackenzie, that this guild was prepared to cooperate in any manner which would further our war effort. Our members now feel however that this declared policy is being taken advantage of.
Then, the next paragraph reads:
In regard to the comparison made by you to ships operated by the Minister of War Transport for Great Britain, this is, so far as we are aware, the first instance of such vesels being compared to Canadian ships in regard to scales of paj- or conditions, as it is well known that in the past British ships have been looked on as being, if not the poorest, at least one of the poorest paid services on the seven seas.
In the wage scale the guild proposed to the Park Steamship company, they pointed out that it was in conformity with the wage scale then in effect on the Pacific coast on vessels which were much smaller. As a matter of fact, it applied to vessels of less than 4,000 tons, and the scale was considerably less than that on United States ships.
In regard to crews, the rates of pay are very much below those on similar ships operating on the Pacific coast. I have before me a list of the rates, as given to me by the officers of the seamen's union, and I shall place them on record for purposes of comparison. In both cases bonuses are not included, but in any event bonuses on the Pacific coast would make the total wage still higher.
The following is a comparison of rates paid on the Pacific coast and those paid by the Park Steamship company:

When the government is attempting to build up a Canadian merchant marine which will operate not only during the war but after the war, we should surely try to make working conditions for the men who will operate these boats have some relation to conditions on privately-operated ships both in this country and in the United States. I should like to know why the government has adopted the British rate rather than the United States rate.

Since merchant seamen come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport I shall try to give the hon. member some explanation. It is well known that the basic rate for seamen on foreign going ships has never been uniform. I am informed that the United States rate has always been higher than the British rate. When the seamen were hired to man Canadian ships a Canadian basic rate was tentatively established with the idea of conforming as much as possible to the British rate. The United Kingdom basic rate for able seamen is $62.02, with a war risk bonus of $44.50, making a total of $106.52. The basic rate paid by the' Park Steamship company for 10,000-ton ships is $56.20, to which is added a war risk bonus of $44.50, a cost-of-living bonus of $18.42, making a total rate of $119.12, as compared with the British rate of $106.52.
What is the United States rate?
So far as we have been able to understand, there is really no basic rate.
Does the minister know what the Pacific coast rate is?

It varies according to the vessel and the trade and the route and the company. Of course there are union rates on the Pacific coast, and they bear more relation to the United States rates than do the basic rates established for British seamen and the tentative Canadian rates. The Canadian rate has never been definitely established. The
War Appropriation-Supplies

matter has been referred to the war labour board for adjustment and ruling, and that is where the matter stands at the present time.
Mr. MadNNIS: When was the matter referred to the war labour board?

I have not the exact date of the reference, but I know the matter has been under consideration. There has been a lot of correspondence and negotiation, and that is the action that has been decided upon.

Why was it necessary to keep the Canadian rate down to the British rate? In making his statement the other day, the Minister of Munitions and Supply said in effect that Canada could have as many ships in her merchant navy as she could man, that the bottleneck was getting crews. It may be that this is one reason why you cannot get crews. The wages on this continent are higher than those in Great Britain; the wages paid in the United States merchant navy are higher than those paid in the British merchant navy. Why should Canada be restricted to the rates paid in the British merchant navy?
I wish my hon. friend would quote me. I said the difficulty was in obtaining qualified officers.

The minister is reported at page 3550 of Hansard as follows:
The United Kingdom is able to furnish crews for these boats whereas Canada cannot do so at this time.
Every effort is being made to obtain the maximum number of crews for the purpose of operating as many ships as possible by Park Steamship Company, and in that connection the company works closely with the director of merchant seamen, Department of Transport, During the war period the size of the Park Steamship Company fleet will be limited only by the number of Canadian crews that can be obtained.
There is the story.

I am quite sure that I explained on another occasion that it was possible to train seamen, but it was impossible to train captains and chief engineers in a short period. As my hon. friend knows, in order to qualify as a captain or a chief engineer a man must have at least four or five years service on a ship. Certain other officers also require a considerable period of service on a ship. Even an ordinary seaman must have four months on a ship to qualify. He signs on as a boy and comes back from his first voyage an able seaman. We can make seamen and we can make officers to the extent of the time at our disposal. We have officers' training schools, but our difficulty is in producing certificated captains, certificated first officers,

certificated chief engineers and perhaps certificated firemen. These we are borrowing in part from the British mercantile marine, and the British mercantile marine are willing to lend them to us, provided that our scale of wages for officers is identical with theirs.
For officers?
For officers.
What about the men?
The scale for the men is higher on Canadian ships than it is on British ships.
Not very much.
It is higher.

How far is it intended to carry this policy of tying the rates paid to Canadian seamen to the rates paid to British seamen? We have been told in this house in the last few weeks that Canada is going to build up a merchant navy. Do the present rates mean that after the war the Canadian rate is to be tied to the lower British rate? If that is to be done, we may have a whole lot of trouble in building up a merchant navy.
We shall have four times the trouble if my hon. friend keeps agitating against the present policy.

The minister need not fly off the handle and start calling people agitators and everything else. Apparently there is only one person in this house and that is the minister himself. He might give somebody else credit for having a few good motives.

The hon. member for Vancouver South realizes that we are just pioneering in building up crews for our merchant ships. We have not been able to secure officers in Canada and we get them from the British merchant service. Fortunately we are building up our own engineers and mechanics. We have two schools

War Appropriation-Supplies
in Canada, but we have not yet reached the stage where we can give instructions in the higher class of engineering and consequently we get these engineers from the British service. We have been successful so far through an understanding with the British government. We are happy to be in that position. But we hope to develop our training facilities to the point where we shall be able to give the initial training in Canada and enable our boys to graduate and eventually reach the stage where they will be capable of taking full charge of our merchant ships. I do not want the hon. member to misunderstand me. There is no move to tie up the rate of pay for Canadian seamen to the rate of pay in the British merchant navy. There is already quite a difference. A second officer in the British merchant navy gets $148.60 a month and in the Canadian merchant navy $192.90 a month. There is a differentiation so far between the United States rate of pay and the British rate of pay. The whole matter is in the process of pioneering. We are doing the best we can to get the crews and pay them a rate that wall satisfy them and at the same time meet the shipping conditions that have so far prevailed in Canada.

The Minister of Transport has said that we are pioneering in this field and trying to attract men who would serve as officers and crews on our boats. If we want to attract men to serve as officers and crews on these boats, I think the best way to do so would be to .pay reasonable wages, wages that would have some relation to the wages which are being paid for similar work on this continent. The minister will not attract Canadians to this work unless he pays Canadian wages. If he is going to keep the wage rates at the British standard he will have to depend for all time on British sources for his officers and crews. He will not get Canadians under those circumstances if they can find work anywhere else. When I hear the Minister of Transport speak in regard to this matter and take into consideration what the Minister of Munitions and Supply said the other day in regard to the Aluminum company, I am forced to the conclusion that the Canadian merchant seamen's guild and the seamen's union are not in a position to demand what the Aluminum company was in a position to demand. The company had the bulge on the minister and on the people of Canada and they used it. But the seamen were patriotic enough not to press for all that they could demand because their country was at war. Consequently they feel that
advantage has been taken of their willingness to serve. What is the rate of pay for deck officers on the Pacific coast?
I am sorry I have not that information before me. This matter has come up unexpectedly, but I shall have the information when my war estimates are before the house.

This item for cargo vessels is of the utmost importance to those Canadians who live on the Pacific slope, and in fact it has become of the utmost importance to the whole of Canada. The Minister of Munitions and Supply very properly said the other day when he was making his statement that the development in our cargo shipbuilding represents the achievement of building up what is virtually a new major industry for Canada. He went on to point out that there are now 43,000 men and women in this country engaged in building merchant ships. Of that number I believe that over half are working on the Pacific coast, where we are making the majority of these cargo vessels. We have also been told within the last two or three weeks that Canada is going to build up a merchant navy and a substantial naval fleet which will include not only escort vessels but such capital ships as cruisers and possibly submarines. We have also been told something of the ship repairs that are being made in Canada in our various shipyards, and of course there will be more and more of this. In addition to the plants engaged in shipbuilding itself, there are many plants making components for the ships; that is the position on the Pacific coast.
But there, and I am sure all members from British Columbia will agree with me in this, we are greatly concerned as to the permanency of this large industry. In the last-war we saw a shipbuilding industry built up there, and then after the war it died right away until there was practically nothing left. We are afraid that something of the same sort will happen after this war unless steps are taken by the government to prevent it. Most of the shipbuilding plants and the industries manufacturing components for ships are dependent largely on steel, and at the present time we are in an unnatural position, in that our steel has to be hauled from eastern Canada or the Eastern United States, and our scrap iron cannot be used on the coast, but is being sent back east under a freight rate which amounts, I believe, to $13 a ton. Therefore, as I say, the situation is unnatural, and unless something is done to change it,

War Appropriation-Supplies

the whole shipbuilding industry may collapse; in fact, it may not be able to carry on at its present capacity during the war itself.
We believe that there should be established on the Pacific an iron and steel industry. We believe that it is a natural industry for that coast, and we would ask the help of the ministry, and hon. members from other parts of Canada in seeing that such an industry is established there eventually. We have the iron and the coal from which to make the coke, and we have the limestone. The provincial government of British Columbia has been greatly concerned over this question for some years, and particularly during the last session. For many years there has been an act on the provincial statute books which provides subsidies to anyone who will establish a steel industry. I believe two million dollars is available for the purpose now. Last year our government had a report made by engineers from the United States, named Arthur G. McKee and Company, on the question of whether we had the iron ore and also the coal and limestone with which to establish the industry. I find in the report of this firm, at page 23, the following:
The principal raw material requirements for the 75,000-ton plant would be iron ore, coking coal and limestone. These are available in ample amounts and suitable quality on Vancouver island and in the interior of the province. Vancouver island is recommended as a preferable location for the plant because of its more central location with respect to the principal consumers and its facilities for transportation by water.
In addition to this iron ore at the coast, there are several million tons of iron concentrates which have been stored by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company, to which the hon. member for Kootenay West made reference this afternoon, at their Sullivan mine, located at Kimberley in east Kootenay. From that wonderful mine they get three products: lead, zinc and iron. They are using the lead and the zinc and storing the iron concentrates right there on the spot. That is only a few miles away from splendid coking coal in the Crowsnest pass, which is also in the east Kootenay district.
So that, I repeat, we believe that the iron and steel industry is a natural industry for British Columbia; that it can be made permanent if the government gives help; and we would like to know what the government is prepared to do, whether or not it will give any help. For example, will it consider a subvention to assist in the establishment of a steel and iron industry? We feel that eastern interests are against the project. The hon. member for New Westminster mentioned that
the other day, and the opinion expressed by him is held, I believe, by the other members from British Columbia. Therefore we ask assistance from the dominion government. The Minister of Munitions and Supply has already broken ground in establishing a policy of this type, by what was done with regard to Steep Rock. Earlier this evening I read to the committee from a press release made by the Department of Munitions and Supply on September 20, 1942, which stated:
Mr. Howe announced that the policy of assistance rvas decided upon as a result of a decision of the war committee of the cabinet that the development of the Steep Rock iron ore deposits should be proceeded with as a means of protecting Canada against a possible shortage of iron ore to meet war requirements.
I have no objection to that help being given. I think it is a wonderful thing to assist the development of iron mines anywhere in Canada, for I suggest that there are some very weak pillars in the edifice which we Canadians are building. One was mentioned this evening; it is that we do not manufacture aeroplane engines. I believe every hon. member will agree that that is a tragedy. It may not be practical to do so; the fact nevertheless remains that it is a tragedy. Another weakness is that we are short of coal; we do not produce enough to keep ourselves warm in the winter. We have had a very sharp taste of what that means during the past winter, and it, too, is a weakness in our Canadian economy. Another is that we produce very little iron. Let there be no mistake about it; that is one of the weaknesses of our Canadian economy. These deficiencies have become clearly visible during the war, and we should exert every effort to make them good. So I urge upon the government that it adopt the definite policy of offering inducements which will help in the establishment of an iron and steel industry on the Pacific coast. It is a matter on which there is no division of opinion; all the people of our province, whether Liberals, Conservative, C.C.F. or Social Creditors, are keen that something should be done along this line. I am afraid that the industry cannot be started without help from Ottawa. I ask the minister to give us some idea of the views of the government on this question.

I was approached early in the war regarding a steel industry for British Columbia. I then stated that the first essential of starting a steel project was to get expert management, and that without expert management nothing could be done. I said that the second problem was to get capital interested. I promised that if the expert management was

War Appropriation-Supplies
obtained and certain local capital was provided, the government would be prepared to examine the situation very carefully with a view toward participation. That offer has never been withdrawn. It was repeated recently.
That is, for a rolling mill or a regular steel industry?
Either one.
That would apply also to a proper steel industry?

Quite. That has been an open offer. I would point out to my hon. friend that Steep Rock was not organized by the government. It was organized by private interests, who spent a great deal of work and money in preliminary examination. They went out and got their management and their finance, and came to the government and said, "We cannot compete for this reason," and the government met the lack in that regard, which was lack of transportation.
It is a little easier for them to do that in the east than it is on the coast.
I cannot say about that, but I know that every steel industry in eastern Canada was started, not by government capital, but by private capital and private initiative.
Well, but they are more firmly established in eastern Canada.
Could the minister say how much capital would be required to establish a workable project?

You have a splendid industry established in your great province, a steel rolling mill of the type discussed for Vancouver. I suppose the capital invested in that is about a million dollars. If we are talking about steel, from the ore to the finished product, at least $40,000,000 would be required initially and probably considerably more before it was through. The report was made on it and the suggestion was that $36,000,000 would be the minimum.
The McKee report sets out between $16,000,000 and $17,000,000.
That is for a small beginning, a blast furnace.
Are cargo vessels built in Canada burning coal, or have you any burning oil?

The North Sands type are coal burning and the Victory type oil burning, and plans are now being made for the production of a modified North Sands type which will have provision for burning either coal or oil.
72537-239J

The government has contributed a great deal of capital to the establishment of certain industries connected with the war. I have the impression that it has put a great deal of money into various private industries.

No. The government has not put money into private industry, but has built government facilities to be operated by private industry. It has not financed private industry. It is unfortunate that the words "capital assistance" have been used to describe expenditures of this kind. Expenditures for increased industrial expansion are, in ninety-nine cases out of 100, built for the account of the government and are retained in the ownership of the government.

What seems difficult for us in the west to understand is why the government does not contribute capital to the establishment of a steel industry in British Columbia. 1 sympathize strongly with the people from British Columbia. I do not believe that industiy is being conducted for the good of the country. In Ontario and Quebec, where industry is being centralized, the people will ultimately be among the greatest sufferers. Every effort should be made to decentralize industry, and for that reason I do think the government should do more than make an offer. They should actually make an endeavour to establish a steel industry in British Columbia.

Has the government considered providing for a subvention on iron ore produced in the west? It might help in the opening up of iron mines. The provincial government have some provision for assistance, and it might be a great help if the dominion would do something similar.
The dominion government have never subsidized iron ore. They are not subsidizing iron ore anywhere at the moment.
It is a fact, is it not, that Canada is very short of iron ore and will be in the future?
No one at the moment is short of anything. British Columbia is not short of steel and Canada is not short of iron ore. We are doing all right.
We are using United States iron ore at the moment.
Yes.

I do not quite understand the minister when he speaks about the unfortunate term "capital assistance". In Votes
War Appropriation-Supplies

and Proceedings of Friday, March 26, we have a list of companies that have been assisted- page after page of them. There must be hundreds of them. Surely all these companies mentioned do not belong to the government.
Yes, they do. The companies do not, huit the assets created by the money shown opposite the companies belong to the government, whether it be machinery or buildings or land.
And do I understand that none of this represents expansion of the firms themselves?
The firms are using it, either machine tools or the building created at the government's expense, but it belongs to the government and it will be reclaimed by the government after the war.
But it does result in expansion of the company for the present.
Yes.

I am interested in the question of Canadian seamen. The Minister of Transport is in his place, and there are a few questions I wish to ask him. The Minister of Munitions and Supply stated that the problem now is not getting ships but getting men to man the ships. I discussed this matter recently with a member of the Canadian seamen's union and he pointed out that Canada had lost 3,000 seamen to United States ships on account of the differential that exists between the wage rates, and more and more Canadian seamen are going in that direction. We can understand why. There is a lot of confusion in regard to wage rates as applied to the Canadian merchant navy. For example, the war risk bonus is a matter of agreement between the shipping companies and the seamen. If they are organized, there is some uniformity in the rates; if they happen to be on ships that are not unionized, then the bonus is mot paid in the same way. I do not believe the government has anything to do with the war risk bonus. It is considered a matter of agreement between the seamen and the shipping companies. Second, there is a lot of confusion with regard to the cost-of-living bonus. A certain class of seamen receive it and others do not, and that is something which has not been settled so far as the Department of Labour, and the seamen generally, are concerned. I wish the minister would make some comment on that to show where the matter stands. I had a specific complaint only yesterday in a telegram from the Canadian seamen's union in Halifax, to the effect that a ship engaged in salvage work was

about to start on a four months' trip going into waters which they considered entitled them to the war risk bonus. The bonus does not apply to salvage work within a certain area. This was a four months' trip.
Is that a governmentowned and operated ship, or is it private?

Private. No bonus applies,
but the men are going into waters where the bonus should apply. The company does not pay. It stipulates that if the job is successful, when the men return, half of the risk bonus that applies to other ships in that area will be paid. That is a specific complaint and it may tie up that ship. I tried to get information to-day and succeeded in getting what they had, that as far as the government is concerned there is no authority in the matter. I think it is something that the government will have to interest themselves in. If you allow 3,000 seamen to go into other ships by reason of a difference in wage rates, that is a factor which will have to be taken into account, because there is no use in building ships to carry war materials if the ships cannot be manned. The country is full of war materials, but there is a lack of men to get the material moving. The matter should be clarified. There should be some uniformity on the part of the government.

The hon. member has in mind conditions on privately-owned ships. The figures I gave a few moments ago with regard to basic rates were figures pertaining to government-owned ships, our steamships or those of other branches of government or in the Canadian government merchant navy. I agree that no jurisdiction over the seamen on privately-owned ships is now exercised or attempted to be exercised; that is a matter with which we have not dealt as yet.

That is exactly the point I am making. I do not think there is anything privately owned to-day in Canada, or in any country that wants to prosecute this war successfully. I think any agency that has a definite influence on the progress of the war and is not performing maximum service should be brought under government regulation. In connection with the question of seamen, when the shipment of war materials is definitely retarded by the wage factor I believe the time has arrived when definite regulations should be laid down by the government.

I was late in getting into this argument, but I think my hon. friend knows as well as I do that the matter of seamen's wages comes before the national war labour board. If my memory serves me cor-

War Appropriation-Supplies
rectly, at this moment there are cases of this kind before that board. I think he will agree that this chamber is not the place to adjudicate on wage structures.

I did not make any such suggestion. I was endeavouring to get from the Minister of Transport a clarification of the regulations in regard to the war risk bonus and the cost-of-living bonus, because these are matters which are not understood.

If my hon. friend works in between sessions, even he has a right to go before the national war labour board, as an individual, in regard to wages. When I was chairman of the national war labour board we adjudicated on war risk bonuses and we also did the same with regard to the cost-of-living bonus. I am pointing out what I think the hon. member will admit, from his own experience, that this chamber is not the place to negotiate working conditions when there is an agency that has been set up for that very purpose.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I should like to know what the Minister of Labour thinks this chamber is for if members are not entitled to raise the grievances of their constituents here. At one time I thought the minister was a radical; as a matter of fact I helped to elect him on that basis when he first came into this house.

And my hon. friend almost succeeded in losing that election.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I believe I made a mistake, though I do not make mistakes very often. Now he comes along and says this is not the place to raise questions of wages because, he says, those questions will come before another body.

I did not say that.
Mr. MaeINNIS: The minister said this was not the place to adjudicate upon them. We are not trying to adjudicate upon questions of wages; we are trying to bring grievances to the attention of the ministers, to show them the conditions prevailing in this country. The minister says that anyone can bring a matter to the attention of the national war labour board.

Or the regional board.
Mr. MaeINNIS: That is quite true; but the minister knows as well as I do that before a person can appear and make proper representations before one of these boards, he must have some experience in negotiation, and the ordinary seaman has no such experience. They have to be organized, and even then they can
get their experience only by putting such cases before the boards or by dealing with negotiating committees.

They are fairly well represented; I know their officers fairly well.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I know them too. Those who are organized are represented, and, they have quite capable representatives, but they are not all organized. What has been done here in almost every action by the government has proved conclusively to the workers that they will not get any justice or any considL eration unless they are sufficiently organized to demand it. Then you wonder at strikes. Many of our labour difficulties could be met. before they developed if employers and the government would agree to meet the representatives of the workers and give proper consideration to their requests. It is a strange and dangerous doctrine to put forward in this house that we are not to raise matters affecting the workers here.

It just so happens that my hon. friend is sitting there and we are sitting here. I often wonder how he would run a socialist state on the basis he has been mentioning. My hon. friend was business agent for the street railway union in the city of Vancouver, and he understands as well as I do that negotiations are always the result of a difference of opinion. If you did not have a difference of opinion you would not have two or three or four political parties; if there was not a difference of opinion there would be no need for trades unions. The hon. member gets my point, and if he were sitting here probably he would have to do as we have done; he would set up these agencies like the national war labour board and the regional boards to adjudicate on these things. I wish to say to my hon. friend that I think these boards have done a remarkable job in a big way. They are, however, human institutions; probably they have made mistakes, just as my hon. friend sometimes makes mistakes. I have no doubt he thinks he made a mistake when he came to speak for me in Hamilton; and let me say that we thought we would lose the election after he had been there. But while it is quite logical to bring a grievance before this House of Commons, I do not think this is the place to negotiate trades union agreements.
Mr. MaeINNIS: We are not trying to negotiate trades union agreements here.

I think this discussion is rather outside the item, Mr. Chairman. This item is to provide for the construction of boats, not for their operation. If there is any
International Relief

question in regard to the wages involved in the construction of the boats, that would be quite in order, but I do not think it is in order to raise the question of wages in connection with operating the boats.

The whole matter of the operation of these boats should come up here, because the minister referred to the matter of operation during his statement, and I think we have a perfect right to raise the point on this item.

I wish to ask just one question of the hon. member for Vancouver East, who has just spoken, and the Minister of Labour. Who is true to the old principles of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group; is it the Minister of Labour or the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group?

Actions speak louder
than words.
Progress reported.
